full_judgment:
6. Question that calls for consideration is whether the presumptive value that the C.S. khatian can be rebuttable by the S.A, khatian prepared under the provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 in the absence of any other evidence. Mr. Bhuiyan submitted that since the S.A, khatian was prepared after hearing objections of the plaintiffs, the High Court,. Division has committed fundamental error in giving the presumptive value to the S.A. Khatians over the S.A. Khatian. In support of his contention he has referred the case of Pramatha Nath Vs. Kamir Mondal, 17 DLR(SC) 392. The second point raised by the learned counsel is that the High Court Division erred in law in interfering with the judgment of the court of appeal below without reversing the findings of fact arrived at by the final court of fact on the question of record of rights. 

 10. To rebut such presumption the defendants have filed only a khatian, the record-of-rights prepared under section 19(3) of the State Acquisition of Tenancy Act, 1950. Except the said khatian, they have failed to produce any other evidence. The court of appeal below held that since the record-of-rights was prepared in the name of the defendants after a contested hearing before the Revenue Officer under section 19(3), the defendants have been able to prove their title in the suit land. There is fallacy in the opinion. The court of appeal below erred in holding the above view for, a record-of-rights prepared under Section 19(3) of the Act of 1950 cannot confer title upon person in whose favour it was prepared. Even the record-of-rights prepared   under the repealed section 143A cannot be the basis of title to the land. It may be used for collateral purpose of possession.   If the views taken by the court of appeal view are accepted, no litigant will be required to take shelter to the civil court for establishing the right, title and interest in the suit land. 

 11. Section 19 is included in Part IV, Chapter IV under the heading preparation of 'record-of-rights' The said Chapter contains sections 17 to 31 Section 17 provides for preparation of record-of-rights prepared or revised of the interests of all rent-receivers as are liable to be acquired under the provisions of the Act of 1950 with a view to the assessment of compensation payable for all such interests including the interests which have already been acquired under. Chapter II It was held in the Province of Province of East Pakistan V Muhammad Hossain Mia, 16 DLR(SC)667 that the notification contemplated under section 17(3) of the Act was a notification giving notice to the intention of Government to take up preparation of new record-of-rights for the assessment of compensation payable for the interests acquired under the Act, and has a conclusive evidence that the order has been made for the preparation or revision record-of-rights. 

 12. Section 18 says, the particulars should be recorded in the record-of-rights. When a draft record-of-rights prepared or revised under section 19(1) containing particulars referred to in section 18, the publication of the draft is with a view to receive and consider any objection that may be made as regards any entry in the record-of-rights. The finality referred to in sub-section (3) of section 19 which shall have conclusive evidence is for the purpose of payment of compensation and the court cannot draw any presumption other than that There is no presumption of possession of land in respect of record-of-rights prepared under section 19(3) like the one under section 103B of the Bengal Tenancy Act. Reference in this connection are the cases of Halima Begum V. Syed Ahmed, 21 DLR 854, Chan Mahmood (Md) V. Md. Hossain Ali, 3 BLC 364, Abdul Kader Bari V. Kaiser Ahmed Howlader, 4 BLC 17, Ahmed Meah V. Abdul Majid, BLD 1985 (HCD)47, Md. Naimuddin Sarder V. Abdul Kalam Biswas, 39 DLR(AD) 237. In Halima Begum the preemptor claimed pre-emption as co-sharer on the strength of record-an-right prepared under the Act of 1950. It was observed that record-of-right indicates certain right of certain parties but that right is certainly dependent on some material evidence, oral and documentary so as to establish title in favour of persons who claim under the said record of right. The presumption of correctness as to C.S. record of right is not certainly available with regard to State Acquisition Khatians, There is no presumption of correctness in respect of the State Acquisition Khatians.... I add here that certainly there will he presumption of the correctness of the B.S. Khatians prepared or to he prepared after a thorough survey which is under process. 

 14. Section 31 of the Act of 1950 provides that the government may, instead of proceeding under section 17, by notification, in official gazette, order that a compensation assessment roll be prepared under Chapter V in respect of any particular district, part of a district or local area on the basis of the record-of-rights last prepared and finally published under Chapter X of the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 or Chapter IX of the Sylhet Tenancy Act, 1936 without any revision or after revising or recording only such particulars in such record as may be specified in the notification. The repealed provision of section 143A has presumptive value of the record-of-rights cannot be equated with a record-of-rights prepared under section 19 of Act of 1950. 

 15. Under the repealed provision it was provided in sub-section (2) that an application filed under subsection (1) shall be deemed to he a plaint and order passed thereon shall have the force of a decree under Code of Civil Procedure No such language is used in section 19(3) or in section 143B of the Act of 1950. Even a record-of-rights prepared under section 143A which has presumptive value does not confer any title to a litigant on the basis of such record because it is not a suit for declaration of title but it is a proceeding for rectification of mistake of the record-of-rights prepared on the basis of possession in the land in question. So the scheme of the section showed that if a record-of-rights was prepared in pursuance of a decree of a civil court in exercise of powers under section 143A, there is presumption as regards possession of the said land. Reference in this connection are the cases of Assistant Custodian V. Bholanath Ghua and 36 DLR (AD) 79, Riazuddin V. Jatindra Kishore, 37 DLR (AD) 202. Therefore, under no stretch of imagination it can be inferred that by reasons of the record-of-rights prepared under section 19(3) the defendant have acquired title in the land as held by the court of appeal below. 

 16. Next question is whether there was extinguishment of title of the plaintiffs' predecessors in pursuance of the deed of relinquishment (মুক্তিপত্র) exhibit A(1) The court of appeal below held that since Naimuddin admitted in this deed as the adopted son of Karful Bewa and relinquished his right, the plaintiffs could not claim title by way of inheritance and purchase of the property of Karful Bewa and that admittedly Naimuddin was not the legal heir of Karful Bewa. The defendants failed to adduce any legal evidence to prove the C.S. record-of-rights prepared in favour of Karful Bewa other than the record-of-rights prepared under section 19(3) of the Act of 1950. As observed earlier by this record-of-rights no presumption of title can be drawn as is available under section 103B. More so, the suit was remanded to the trial court enabling the defendants to prove মুক্তিপত্র dated 18th December, 1930, exhibit:-A(1) and the A deed dated 17th January, 1935 exhibit-A(2) a deed executed by Toisor Ali in favour of Alimuddin Mondal arid Jamir Ali Mondal. In this deed the executant admitted that the recipients were in possession of the lands over statutory period. The court of appeal below held that Naimuddin extinguished his title by executing these two deeds and therefore the plaintiffs cannot claim any title as heirs of Naimuddin. It misread ext-A(2) for, Naimuddin did not relinquish his title in the lands covered by the deed. This finding is self contradictory with its earlier finding, inasmuch as, Naimuddin being the adopted son of Karful Bewa, he did not inherit her property. More so, after the remand of the suit, the trial court held that though exhibit-B(1) (wrongly mentioned as ext-B(1). It would be ext-A(2) was exhibited but the contents of the deed having not been proved by the defendants in accordance with law, the contents couldn't be looked into; that in proof of exhibit-A (2), the defendants did not produce any in dependent witness and that despite giving opportunity to the defendants, they failed to prove enforceability of exhibit-A(2). It was further observed that the plaintiff Nos. 4 and 5 have been able to prove their title and. possession in the suit land, The court of appeal below has totally over-looked those findings and illegally took exhibits-A(1) and A(2) as the basis of title of the defendants and illegally held that the title of the plaintiffs' predecessor extinguished. In view of the above, the judgment of the court of appeal below is not a proper judgment of reversal.
